Lifting Your Voice


Being a healthcare professional is hard, especially if you don’t know what to expect. We think hearing from you will help give medical students and new healthcare providers a better idea of what to expect. In addition to the responses you have provided, we’d like you to write a letter to a new healthcare provider who will begin working at a medical facility like yours.



In your letter, please describe what you have shared today about providing healthcare in a way that prioritizes patients’ perspectives and meets them where they are. Try to use examples from your own experiences or examples of things you’ve seen.   



Feel free to draw from these themes discussed today:

 

	Research suggests that finding concordance in patient and physician goals promotes patient self-efficacy –patients believe that they have the capacity to execute behaviors necessary to improve their health. 
	Small changes in a physician’s practice can vastly improve patient trust in medical care – such as adopting a patient-centered approach in healthcare visits. 
	Sensitivity toward the circumstances that might get in a patient’s way along their journey toward maximized health allows the patient to be active in their healthcare, increasing compliance and long-term well-being.


 

Please respond with at least three meaningful sentences to share. Do not worry about spelling or grammar. 

 

 

 

Dear New Healthcare Provider,

column53: Remember that when you see patients, they will be presenting for a number of reasons. Some patients have an acute issue. Some patients are there for chronic conditions. Some patients may be seen for prevention. When you see a patient, you need to take their entire circumstance into consideration. You as the healthcare provider may not initially have all the answers about a person's medical condition after seeing that patient just one time. Try to promote continuity of care with patients and help guide them to help them with their subjective complaints but also guide them through health conditions that they don't necessarily "feel," like high cholesterol. I have found myself throughout the years having to explain to patients, I know you are coming in because you feel "x, y and z" and we will do our best to address those issues. However, you also have other medical conditions that you may not necessary "feel" and these conditions possibly could lead to a number of complications in the future if they are not addressed. Be cautious not just to look at lab results and studies. Listen to your patients. They often may give you clues about what their diagnosis is or how they can be better managed from what they tell you.
column62:
One thing I look at is if a patient is "self pay." I know many other providers I work with don't always pay attention to the patient's health insurance. If I know the patient is paying for the full cost of the medication out of pocket, I will often look up the medication I want to prescribe them on a website like GoodRx. I'll even print the coupon from the website for them and tell them I recommend a certain pharmacy to dispense it because the cost is cheaper there. Obviously, I confirm with the patient that this is the pharmacy they want the script to go to before sending it in.

When there are choices involved in a management plan, I try to explain the different options to the patient using an "RBA" format. If you are unfamiliar with this acronym, it means "risk, benefit, alternative"... I present the various options and go over the "RBA" of each one. That way the patient can make an informed decision about what they want to do. With more complex management, sometimes the patient needs longer to think about the various options and in non-acute situations, I encourage a patient to think it over and they do not need to make an immediate decision right there at the time of the encounter.
column67:
A patient has options of doing an iFOBT, a colonoscopy and perhaps a newer option of colon capsule endoscopy for their colon cancer screen. I would describe RBA of each and patient can make informed decision of which one to choose.

Patient lost health insurance and has been taking X medication for a number of years for hypertension. Medication X has a high out of pocket cost when it's not being bought as a formulary medication through a patient's prescription plan. Walmart may have medication Y which is a good alternative to patient X and perhaps it's even on their $4 prescription list. I would present patient with this option so higher chance patient will remain compliant and stay on prescription medication.
column76: When seeing patients with acute issues like a cold (upper respiratory infection) or diarrhea (often a viral gastroenteritis), there is often an attitude from the patient of "doctor, you need to do something." The patient is not feeling well, the patient has a number of life events coming up and they "can't afford" to be ill. The patient's feeling is that the provider needs to prescribe them something so they can get better right away or "nip it in the bud and stop it from getting worse." The quickest way out of the exam room is to just write a prescription for that patient and send them on their way because you basically satisfied their rationale for wanting to come for an appointment that day. It takes more time and use of skills to explain to the patient "that's not the way it works." Most viral illnesses do not have specific medications that "cure" the illness. In most cases, the illness just needs to run its course, and that person needs to relax and let their body do the work to help them get over their illness. There may be some medication that may be prescribed to help alleviate some of the symptoms, but these medications do nothing to make the illness go away any faster or "stop it from getting worse."

column53:
Dear New Practitioner,

You are about to begin a new and challenging phase of you life.  Hopefully you have learned the science and medical teaching well.  Now comes the time when you must interface with individual people of this world.  Each one is unique and has a valuable perspective.  They are usually open to learning from you, given your position.  If I could recommend ideas to you, I'd recommend proposing changes, not imposing them.  These are not your serfs.  They are independent, often talented, people who see things not the way you do.  Propose suggestions.  Offer choices, so they can pick what they are able to do.  If you offer, and don't force, you may be better heard.  

Always offer hope.  Offer people a few different ideas.  Try to keep a "next step" in you back pocket.  When I am out of ideas, then I suggest a specialist.  But I tell them I will stay with them through the process.  I suggest you offer to be their guide, their backstop, the one always in their camp.  I think this approach  may help you bond with patients and give them the choice to be loyal to you.  Sadly, that is rare today, as everyone seems to kick the can down the road.  Be the one who stops the buck with you.

Enjoy people.  Rejoice when you help people reach their goal.  You will get satisfaction and you will help people.

The journey to becoming a provider is not a walk in a park. There will be sweat, tears and sacrifice. It will be filled with questions, doubt, hesitations, regrets. But I assure you that it is a fulfilling endeavor, no matter what field you go into. Healthcare is broad enough to accommodate everyone who is willing to take the first step and push through hardships.

When patients come into my clinic, they seek advice on a particular problem. I want them to leave the clinic feeling they have accomplished more. I want them to leave my room with a partner who will advocate for them no matter what. Despite all the lectures, PowerPoints, books, conferences and exams that we go through, we still have to learn how to interact with people who are not in our field. That, I think is an endeavor in itself, which unfortunately, not all providers realize they lack.

Good luck to your journey!

I definitely have had some patients who really just needed to vent about their medical/health frustrations, and then they've felt better. That's included patients who are desperately searching for causes such as chronic lyme disease or autoimmune disorders who have normal test results. Spending the time to just listen to their frustrations is sometimes what I've found has helped them, despite no clear answers on what's causing their symptoms.
column76:
I have had many instances where patients have started the conversations very anxious, with rushed speech, and many gripes. With some patient listening and asking nonjudgmental and empathetic questions, they have sometimes shown de-escalation with slower and calmer speech. This doesn't always happen, but it's so rewarding when I've seen how helpful it's been for the patient. I've had patients who were disillusioned with traditional medicine tell me that they have faith in the medical profession again. 
It doesn't even always take a lot of time. Sometimes I've found that just quietly and actively listening result in shorter and more fulfilling visits. When I've tried 'shutting things down' quicker, it feels like we both get escalated, and the visit can sometimes last a lot longer.

I hope this message finds you well. I am writing to discuss an important aspect of our healthcare delivery that I believe can significantly enhance patient outcomes and satisfaction: prioritizing patient perspectives and meeting them where they are.
In our practice, we have observed that engaging patients in their care decisions and understanding their unique circumstances can lead to better adherence to treatment plans and overall improved health outcomes. Here are a few strategies we have found effective:
 Active Listening and Empathy: Taking the time to listen to patients' concerns and experiences without interruption helps build trust and rapport. Empathy in our interactions can make patients feel valued and understood.
 Shared Decision-Making: Involving patients in the decision-making process regarding their treatment options ensures that their values and preferences are considered. commitment to the chosen plan.
 Cultural Competence: Understanding and respecting the cultural backgrounds and beliefs of our patients can help tailor our communication and care plans to be more effective and respectful.
 Flexible Care Plans: Recognizing that each patient’s situation is unique, we should be prepared to adapt care plans to meet their specific needs and circumstances. This might include considering their social determinants of health, such as access to transportation, financial constraints, and family support systems.
 Patient Education: Providing clear and accessible information about their conditions and treatment options empowers patients to make informed decisions. Utilizing various educational tools and resources can cater to different learning preferences.
I believe that by incorporating these strategies into our practice, we can create a more patient-centered approach that not only meets patients where they are but also fosters a more positive and effective healthcare experience.
I look forward to discussing this further and exploring ways we can collaborate to enhance our patient care practices.
Best regards,

column62:
As a private practice owner, I give patients my time.  New patient appointments are always booked in 90 minute slots and my shortest follow up appointment is 30 minutes.  I don't want my patients to feel rushed or unheard.  My waiting room has a coffee "bar" that all patients are welcome to use, as well as hot and cold water.  I also keep snacks in my office for patients or their children who need to eat.  I keep various activities such as puzzles, coloring books, stickers, etc that patients and kids can use while they wait, most of which they are free to take with them when they leave.  I have a large "community puzzle" that anyone is free to work on at any time.  My patient bathroom has diapers, wipes and all types of hygiene products available for use and they are free to take items home.  I have a "lending closet" where patients can check out books, learning games, sensory development items and more.  I have my exam room divided into two halves, separated by an accordion wall and the "interview" side has a loveseat for the patients to sit on and there is local art and flowers to look at and they don't have to focus on all the medical equipment.  I have a "spinning chair" that kids (or adults) can use at any time.  I also sit in a comfortable overstuffed chair so that the patient's understand I am not in a hurry, I am here to listen to them and that I do honestly want to get to know them. I have a clock strategically positioned so I can glance at it without making a patient feel rushed.  I have my entire office/exam area set up intentionally with complex trauma in mind.  I don't sit between patients and the door, the couch is against a wall so no one can sneak up on them, patients can see all the doors when they walk in a room, I have white noise to help with sound hypervigilance.  Unless a patient is in the patient bathroom, I keep the door open so patients can reassure themselves no one is in there. Initially I hated having a laptop between me and the patient, but as time went on, especially after covid started, I found sending prescriptions/orders/referrals while sitting in the patient room not only was more efficient, but patients feel empowered to advocate for themselves with labs and pharmacies when they claim they hadn't received the orders (a very common and serious problem in my rural area). One of the most important things I find my patients value is a very simple (non)policy.  I do not have a "missed appointment" or "no show" policy.  If a patient no shows or doesn't call or misses an appointment or cancels after the fact, it is not a problem.  I go out of my way to never make them feel guilty or judged. 
 There is no charge and I will not "fire" a patient for missing appointments. And appointments can be converted to telemedicine even if they were scheduled in person.  For many of my patients with mental health issues, telemedicine has changed their lives, allowing them to have appointments even when their symptoms are too severe to leave their homes.  This very simple policy which really is not of any consequence to me, has increased trust and improved patient relationships in numerous ways.
column67: My very rural, very poor patient population has significant social and economic stressors.  I had a young patient show up to their appointment with their toddler and both of them were crying and soaking wet.  Her car had died that morning and she really wanted to make it to the well child appointment because she was afraid DHS would punish her if she missed another appointment.  So she packed up her toddler and walked to the appointment in the pouring rain, forgetting the diaper bag in the back of her dead car.  She walked into my office sobbing and the toddler was screaming and in desperate need of a clean diaper.  I grabbed them both towels and told her to sit down and catch her breath.  I took the toddler, stripped him of his wet clothes and dirty diaper and gave him a warm bath in the bathroom sink. I got him into a clean diaper and wrapped him in a dry towel.  Both of them were hungry and she couldn't get to the store with a dead car and there is none in our town.  There is a food pantry in our building and I sent her there while I fed the toddler some of the snacks I keep on hand.  When she returned with her groceries, I asked her if she still wanted to do the well child appointment and she did.  We did that and I did a referral for early intervention and set her up with our local Parents as Teachers organization where she can get free supplies as incentives for participating in activities, going to WIC or well child appointments, etc.  When the appointment was over, my assistant drove her and the toddler and their bags of groceries home so she didn't have to walk in the rain again.  By tending to their immediate physical needs, I was able to build more trust and calm some anxiety.  By referring her to Parents as Teachers, I am empowering mom to become more self-sufficient as well as improving her ability to be a successful parent. By doing all of it in a genuine empathetic manner, I reminded mom of her worth and instilled confidence in her abilities.

Congratulations on reaching this pivotal moment in your career! Starting your journey as a healthcare provider is both exciting and daunting. You’ve spent years preparing for this, and now, you’ll finally put your knowledge into practice. While your medical education has equipped you with the skills to diagnose and treat, there’s an essential aspect of healthcare that goes beyond clinical knowledge—the art of truly connecting with your patients and meeting them where they are.

When I first started, I was eager to demonstrate everything I’d learned. But soon, I realized that the most effective care comes from understanding not just the illness but the person behind it. Patients come from all walks of life, with diverse backgrounds, beliefs, and expectations. It's easy to get caught up in the clinical side of things, but the heart of healthcare is empathy and connection.

I remember one patient vividly—a middle-aged man who had been diagnosed with diabetes. He had missed several appointments and wasn’t following his treatment plan. It would have been easy to label him as “non-compliant” and move on. But instead, I took the time to listen. I learned that he worked two jobs, had limited access to healthy food, and was overwhelmed by the complexities of managing his condition. By understanding his perspective, we were able to tailor a treatment plan that fit his life. We focused on small, achievable goals, and I connected him with resources that made healthy choices more accessible. Over time, he became more engaged in his care, and his health began to improve.

It is important to try your best to fully explain their diagnosis and all treatment options (risks, benefits, etc) at their level, and then come up with the treatment plan that they are most comfortable with and not be paternalistic in your approach.  For instance, I often give patients/family the option to empirically treat an injury based on their history, physical exam, x-ray findings (or lack thereof), and my experience and then get an MRI later if they don't get better, versus getting an MRI right away (if insurance authorizes) and then coming up with a treatment plan after the MRI.  I want to do what makes the patient or parents most comfortable and gives them the most re-assurance, including taking finances into consideration - if they can't afford or don't want to pay the MRI co-pay/deductable, then that is fine as long as I feel it is safe to hold off on getting an MRI. column53: Remember, what made you want to be a physician? Not everyone is booksmart like us so we do need to be cognizant of how we speak to our patients as well. I always believed in treating others the way we want to be treated, and so with that in mind, being sensitive to our patients’ shame, fear, anxiety, or any other emotion you can see on their face or their voice, will truly guide you in the right direction as you continue to practice the most difficult of jobs — being a primary care physician — having to answer to every question that a patient has about their health and not health, as well as the health of their family members, and being bombarded with all the quality metrics that you must make sure is covered, while addressing their 15 problems that they want you to help them with.

column53: Medicine is exciting.  Learning about the body and treatments is great.  You will be seen as a leader of your community.  People will talk about you, because you hold a title.  That is exciting at first...then it can feel like a burden at times.  Combined with the need to see many patients in a day and try to balance the changes in life that tend to come around the time you start practice (growing families for example), it is easy to get away from that excitement and desire to get to know your patients.  Ask any doctor who has been in practice for a decade and often they say the thing that keeps them happy and going is getting to know their patients.  However, in hospital settings (with many primary care docs in the employment model) there are pressures to see a certain number of patients.  Please be strong, you can have some control over your schedule, even if it seems like you do not.  Ask your staff to schedule 30 minute appointments for the patients who often want to talk. Welcome to the world of direct patient care. It is scary and overwhelming, but with time becomes fulfilling and manageable. It is very easy to lose sight of what your job is when you get bogged down in the daily tasks that need to be done. It is important to take a step back and remember that you are taking care of a human, and to see patients as people and not units of work. Often the most rewarding part of healthcare is connecting with a patient and watching your interventions make a difference in their life. 

One thing that has helped me tremendously has been to learn about not just the medical parts of a patient, but also their social history. Where they live, what they do, their familial and personal relationships, and their goals in life play a huge role in how they view healthcare. Anticipating and identifying barriers to treatment will go a long way towards taking better care of your patients.
column62: One way I try to connect with patients is to ask them where they are from and about their hometown. I also ask about family they have or hobbies they take part in. Then when I see them on subsequent visits, I’ll bring up what we discussed last time to show that I remember them as a person and have invested in them and their health. I also try to be as honest with patients as possible, and tell them candidly what I’m thinking and what their medical problems are. If I don’t know something, I will admit it to them, but also say that I will look into it for them. I feel that being open and honest lets them see my human side as well, which helps foster a relationship between us.

column53:
Welcome to practice of Medicine.  Our profession is not as glamorous as they portray it on the TV screen.  A lot of personal and family sacrifices have to be made. There will be many last minute cancellations of family activities due to emergency calls. It is a high stress profession as people’s lives depend on you. Your medical decisions will be life changing for a lot of the patients so we have to be very judicious when we advise our patients and make medical recommendations. However, we also have the opportunity to help them feel better about themselves, to help them get healthier and able to spend more time with their friends and loved ones.  Some patients may be confrontational when they come to see you, but it would be prudent to bear in mind that they may already be having a very bad day at home and they are worried about their medical issues. Show compassion, patience, and honesty when taking care of the patients. Remember that one day, we will be a patient too, and we would want our doctor to exhibit these qualities. 

Foods for thought:
1. Treat others the way you would like to be treated.
2. Respect is not demanded.  It is earned. 
3. When treating patients with complicated issues, remember that it is more fortuitous to be on the treating (giving) side than the receiving end. 

LET US GO AND SAVE SOME LIVES!!!

A common phrase among healthcare workers is, “healthcare is a team sport.” This is definitely true regarding interdisciplinary care, but I also think perhaps the most important “team” forms between the provider and the patient (and their families).
Taking the extra time to get to know your patients outside of their diagnosis, identify their hesitations and baseline understandings, and form longitudinal relationships (whether this is just over the course of their hospital stay, or over several years of seeing the patient in the clinic) increases patient buy-in and sense of agency over their health. 
Always remember, you may see 20 patients in a day, but each of those patients is (usually) only seen one doctor. The handful of minutes you spend with each one can change the trajectory of not only their day, but also their life.
column62:
I tried to learn a little bit about every single patient’s non-medical history, such as what they do or did for a living, what they enjoy to do in their free time, Their children or spouses names, Etc. I tried to make note of these in a secure location within the EMR and refresh myself on these details prior to my next appointment with the patient. Typically a very personal connection, and helps patient to realize that I really do care about them as people rather than just another office visit or prescription to write.
Additionally, I try to explain in non-medical terms what their medication’s do and what they are treating. I like to explain the medical reasoning behind certain prescriptions, if applicable — for example, for a patient with a new diagnosis of heart failure I always included discussion of important medication’s that we will be initiating over the next several office visits and I highlight/emphasize the reason behind the specific medication’s that data actually shows they will prolong this patient’s life and improve their quality of life. That helps patients have more buy-in for medically necessary therapies as well as helps them understand that I’m not writing prescriptions just to satisfy “Big Pharma” but because they have a real and measurable impact on the patient’s life.
column67: Just yesterday when I was in the clinic, a patient came in for a follow-up visit after about four months. She informed me that she “stopped all her medication’s because she “was sick of taking alll those pills and had taken them for 35 years.” She appeared apologetic and fearful of how I would respond to her “ignoring the doctor’s advice.” I emphasized that I understood the burden over a dozen daily pills could have on a person, and understood her desire to cut back. I reinforced her decision to cut out unnecessary pills and prescriptions. I’ve been reviewed each medication she stopped taking with her directly; after a thorough review, I suggested she restart only two of the 10 medication’s because they had the most evidence that they would protect her from worsening health outcomes long-term, and actually prolong her life. After this discussion, the patient was happy to receive those two medications, and even even happier that I didn’t make feel guilty or bad about discontinuing the others.

I found that this continuity of care increases their trust and comfort with the healthcare system, as well as with our practice. It's been a long road. There will be happy times when you know what you have done is for a patient's greater good because VOILA!, they are cured! The reality is that there will be troubles that you only read in the news and things just so bizarre. Stay cool. Fret not, take a deep breathe and learn how to listen without saying I'm sorry. Sorry is what you say when you want permission to stop feeling bad. A pt. doesn't want to hear you say sorry, a lot of them want you to say what can be done, how he/she can gear up for the battle that awaits. And while the gear is good, there are times when that gear needs changes and each battle is a different story. Each battle doesn't lessen their fear, their anxiety so It's up to you to help them play it out at all defensive/offensive positions. So get ready, know how to play. 
All you have to do is listen and make sure your patient is heard. If you get that down, that's half the battle. 
One more thing, know to take of yourself. Love yourself and know when you can't do this. Take the time out to stare out of the window and look out at the sky. It is a beautiful world after all. Appreciate yourself and what you do. As a side note, Thank you for all you do, for those pt's that might not say thank you. Because those exist as well. Last, You are here for a reason and the rewards of a smile, of trust from someone you didn't know 5 minutes ago, is priceless. 
All the best to you.

As you navigate the busy field of healthcare, always keep these tenants in mind:
Never pass up an opportunity for patients to direct their care when several options of equal outcome exist.  As these decisions affect them the most, allowing for shared decision making is a powerful way to build trust.
Allowing patients and families to define their priorities will provide insight as to how to structure their treatment plan, gain trust, and remove barriers.
Proving medical knowledge and insights good, but also support, reassurance, and proving a safe forum for patients to be heard and feelings validated brings a humanistic element that is required for success in medicine, and devoid in much of today’s culture.

It is privilege to have the trust, insight, and impacts on so many people’s lives…. Use it wisely.

column28: Understanding patients' perspectives and their reasons for their actions is critical because it allows healthcare providers to offer more personalized and effective care. This understanding fosters trust, improves communication, and enhances patient compliance with treatment plans. column33:
Understanding a patient's perspective can have a significant positive influence on both the patient and their recovery. When healthcare providers take the time to truly understand a patient’s feelings, beliefs, and motivations, it helps in building a strong therapeutic relationship based on trust and mutual respect. This connection can make patients feel heard, valued, and supported, reducing anxiety and increasing their willingness to engage in their treatment plan.

Additionally, understanding their perspective allows providers to tailor interventions that align with the patient’s values and lifestyle, making it more likely for them to adhere to the recommended treatments. It also enables healthcare providers to address any barriers or concerns the patient may have, such as fear of side effects or cultural hesitations, thus improving compliance. Overall, this approach not only enhances the patient’s emotional well-being but also promotes active participation in their own care, leading to improved recovery rates and better overall health outcomes.
column42:
Patients may feel anxious or hesitant to ask questions for several reasons. Commonly, they might fear that their questions will seem silly or that they’ll be judged for not understanding medical jargon or complex information. Some patients worry about taking up too much of the healthcare provider’s time, especially if they perceive that the provider is busy or rushed. There can also be a power dynamic at play, where patients feel intimidated or uncomfortable challenging the authority of a healthcare professional.

Cultural factors may also contribute; in some cultures, questioning a doctor is considered disrespectful. Additionally, past negative experiences with healthcare providers, where patients felt dismissed or not listened to, can make them reluctant to speak up. Finally, anxiety or embarrassment about their health condition can make patients feel vulnerable, leading them to hold back on asking questions they genuinely want answers to. Understanding these reasons is crucial for healthcare providers to create a more open, supportive environment that encourages patient engagement and communication.

I recall working with a patient who was visibly anxious and hesitant to engage during her appointments. She was dealing with a chronic condition that required lifestyle changes, but she was struggling to follow through with the recommendations. Instead of focusing solely on the medical aspects of her care, I took a step back and made an effort to center her as a person, not just a patient. I began by asking open-ended questions about her life—her family, work, and what she enjoyed doing in her free time. 

Through these conversations, I learned that she was overwhelmed with her responsibilities at home, which made it difficult for her to prioritize her health. She shared stories about her children and her worries about being a burden to them. By listening without judgment and acknowledging her concerns, I was able to show her that I genuinely cared about her as an individual. This approach helped build trust, and over time, she became more comfortable sharing her fears and asking questions about her care. 

We worked together to develop a plan that accommodated her lifestyle, focusing on small, manageable steps rather than overwhelming changes. By centering the patient, getting to know her personally, and building trust, she felt more supported and empowered, which significantly improved her adherence to the treatment plan and ultimately her health outcomes. This experience reinforced the importance of truly seeing and hearing the patient beyond their medical condition.

Today, we explored the concept of delivering healthcare that truly prioritizes patients' perspectives and meets them where they are. This approach is not just about treating an illness, but about engaging with patients in a way that acknowledges their individual experiences and circumstances.

Research shows that when patients and physicians align on healthcare goals, patients feel more empowered and believe in their ability to manage their health. For instance, if a patient with diabetes and their doctor collaboratively set realistic goals, such as incorporating more fruits and vegetables into the diet rather than aiming for drastic lifestyle changes all at once, the patient is more likely to follow through. This concordance fosters a sense of self-efficacy, making patients feel more capable of managing their condition effectively.

I've seen firsthand how small changes in practice can significantly enhance patient trust. For example, one doctor I observed made it a point to ask open-ended questions during consultations and actively listened to the patient's responses before offering medical advice. This patient-centered approach not only made the patient feel heard but also helped build a stronger therapeutic alliance. The patient felt more comfortable discussing concerns and preferences, which led to more tailored and effective care.

Sensitivity to the barriers patients face on their health journey is crucial for fostering long-term well-being. Consider a situation where a patient struggles with adherence to a medication regimen due to side effects or financial constraints. A healthcare provider who acknowledges these challenges and works with the patient to find alternative solutions—such as exploring different medication options or connecting the patient with financial assistance resources—can significantly improve compliance and outcomes. By understanding and addressing these practical obstacles, healthcare providers empower patients to be more active participants in their care.

In summary, prioritizing patients' perspectives means engaging with them on their terms, setting shared goals, and addressing their unique challenges with empathy and practical solutions. This approach not only enhances trust and adherence but also contributes to better overall health outcomes.

column53:
Welcome to our medical group.  We look forward to having you become an important member of our team and learning from one another.  We are focused on providing quality care to all our patients.  Your training program provided you with many of the clinical skills that you will rely upon and enhance throughout your career.  Our group has always emphasized the need provide patients with patient centered interactions that enhance the physician-patient relationship.  We have developed a "toolbox" to help achieve these goals that we refer to as the 4 E's: Engage, Empathize, Educate and Enlist.  

Engage: Taking the opportunity to connect with every patient at the outset of a visit.  A smile, a friendly comment, some physical contact such as a handshake or pat on the shoulder followed by always sitting down and avoiding focus on the electronic record.  Always asking for permission to look at the EHR briefly or enter data will assure the patient that they are your primary focus.

Empathy:  Expressions of empathy are among the most important interactions you will have with every patient. This skill requires practice for some physicians but will become second nature once fully adopted.  Patients will trust the recommendations you provide if they believe that you truly care about them.  If we interact with every patient as though they were a close family member, expressions of empathy will become more routine.

Educate:  Always talking to patients about their symptoms and concerns in non-medical terminology will make it more likely that they will understand what you are trying to say.  It's always best to never assume that a patient already knows what me mean when we use medical terms.  It never hurts to ask if he or she has any questions about what we expressed.

Enlist:  Developing a plan for the patient's care may seem like the physician's sole responsibility, but it only works when it is a collaborative process.  Asking "Does that sound like something you're willing to do?" is a great way to ensure that the patient will more likely follow it.

Following these simple routines will enhance the quality of your encounters with your patients.  This patient-centered approach will help provide you with a satisfying clinical experience throughout your medical career.

We look forward to working with you to achieve a successful career with our group.

Yours truly,
column62: Every visit can be broken down into 4 categories: How the provider Engages the patient at the onset of the visit.  A warm greeting with a smile.  Sitting down facing the patient and not focusing on the electronic chart.  Beginning with a brief comment or question such as "How has your day been so far?" or "It's good to see you again.  I'm looking forward to catching up with you since our last visit."  Expressing Empathy early in the visit is also essential.  "I'm sorry to hear that your headaches are worse.  Let's see what we can do to help you reduce or eliminate them."  How you Educate the patient is also very important.  Using non-technical language to describe the problem and potential solutions is very important.  Explaining the diagnosis and underlying pathology in terms the patient can easily understand is essential.  Finally, Enlisting the patient in the plan going forward is an equally important part of a quality visit.  It's not "your plan" but a collaborative plan presented to the patient with the patient's consent and agreement.  It does no good for the provider to add a medication or recommend a diet or exercise program if the patient doesn't agree.  In summary, a good visit is made up of the 4 Es:  Engage, Empathize, Educate and Enlist.
column67: My patient, a 67 year old woman, presents for a follow-up visit for her hypertension.  She has been under my care for 8 years and recently widowed. column28: Every patient has their own things that are priority to them in terms of the disease/condition that I am treating which don't necessary align with what I (the provider) am most concerned with. For example, when seeing an elderly patient with diabetes, I am most concerned with the lab values and managing the long term consequences of the disease. However, the patient may be more worried more about the immediate cost of the medications and side effects, and am not really worried about lab values of future problems associated with mismanagement of the disease. If I don't address their concerns of costs and and side effects first, they will likely not even take the medications I prescribe and thus not treat the disease. But, if I do address their concerns, even if it is not ideal treatment plan, I will at least address their concerns and they will be more likely to treat their condition.

First off, welcome to the team! We're thrilled to have you join our medical family. I wanted to share a little something about how we roll here when it comes to taking care of our patients. It's all about meeting them where they are and making sure they feel heard and understood.
